## Claims

### C-R5-001
- **Topic:** 4:4–10 as heart of the letter / prophetic summons  
- **Claim (Moo):** James 4:4–10 is one of the strongest NT calls to repent; though most commentators join it to 4:1–3, Moo judges it has broader scope—OT prophetic denunciation replaces Hellenistic moral-exhortation vocabulary of 3:1–4:3—and gathers the letter’s issues into one all-embracing demand; “Here, if anywhere, we find the heart of James’s letter.”  
- **Quote:** “James gathers up all the specific issues that he deals with in his letter into one all-embracing demand. Here, if anywhere, we find the heart of James's letter.”  
- **Locus:** Moo on Jas 4:4–10 intro; cache ¶1  

### C-R5-002
- **Topic:** “You adulterous people” — feminine form / spiritual adultery  
- **Claim (Moo):** Greek is feminine (“adulteresses”); the KJV’s dual gender form is secondary; not a charge of literal sexual adultery by women, but OT marital imagery (Isa 54:5–6; Jer 3:20; Hosea; Jesus’ “wicked and adulterous generation,” Matt 12:39; 16:4).  
- **Quote:** “The Greek word James uses is actually feminine; see \"adulteresses\" in the NASB. … A literal reading would suggest that James is accusing his female readers of engaging in adulterous sexual activity. But this is unlikely. … The clue to the feminine form and to the accusation that James is making here is found in the OT, especially the prophetic books.”  
- **Locus:** Moo on Jas 4:4; cache ¶2  

### C-R5-003
- **Topic:** Friendship with the world = enmity with God  
- **Claim (Moo):** Following that tradition, James labels readers unfaithful people of God; friendship with the world is spiritual adultery. Hellenistic friendship meant “sharing all things” in spiritual and physical unity (Johnson), so choosing friendship with the world makes one “an enemy of God”—hostility of God toward the believer as well as of the believer toward God.  
- **Quote:** “By seeking friendship with the world, they are, in effect, committing spiritual adultery. … Anyone who chooses to be a friend of the world becomes an enemy of God. \"Enemy,\" especially in light of the OT background we have cited, must involve hostility of God toward the believer as well as that of the believer toward God.”  
- **Locus:** Moo on Jas 4:4; cache ¶3  

### C-R5-004
- **Topic:** Worldly imitation without overt apostasy  
- **Claim (Moo):** Readers were not overtly disclaiming God, but discrimination (2:1–13), negative speech (3:1–12), bitter envy/selfish ambition (3:13–18), and destructive pleasures (4:1–3) amounted to world-allegiance; “God tolerates no rival.”  
- **Quote:** “We have no evidence that James's readers were overtly disclaiming God and consciously deciding to follow the world instead. But their tendency to imitate the world by discriminating against people (2:1-13), by speaking negatively of others (3:1-12), by exhibiting \"bitter envy\" and \"selfish ambition\" (3:13-18), and by pursuing their own destructive pleasures (4:1-3) amounted to just that. … God tolerates no rival.”  
- **Locus:** Moo on Jas 4:4; cache ¶4  

### C-R5-005
- **Topic:** 4:5 as one of the hardest NT verses / two translation families  
- **Claim (Moo):** Verse 5 explains v. 4 by God’s jealousy demanding total allegiance; yet Jas 4:5 is among the most difficult NT verses. NRSV/NASB/NLT follow divine jealousy; NIV/REB/TEV take human envious longings. No textual variants drive the split—three Greek ambiguities do.  
- **Quote:** “Indeed, Jas. 4:5 is one of the most difficult verses in the NT. … The NRSV, NASB, and NLT follow the line we have laid out above; but the NIV, REB, and TEV take the verse to refer to the jealous longings of human beings.”  
- **Locus:** Moo on Jas 4:5; cache ¶5  

### C-R5-006
- **Topic:** 4:5 two major interpretations stated  
- **Claim (Moo):** Two major options: (1) divine jealousy—“God yearns jealously for the spirit that he has made to dwell in us” (NRSV); (2) human envy—“the spirit he caused to live in us envies intensely” (NIV).  
- **Quote:** “1. James is referring to God's jealousy for his people: \"God yearns jealously for the spirit that he has made to dwell in us\" (NRSV). 2. James is referring to the human tendency to be envious: the spirit he caused to live in its envies intensely (NIV).”  
- **Locus:** Moo on Jas 4:5; cache ¶¶7–8  

### C-R5-007
- **Topic:** 4:5 ambiguity 1 — *pneuma* subject vs object  
- **Claim (Moo):** Neuter *pneuma* can be subject or object of *epipothei*. Human-envy view: spirit = natural human spirit as subject. Divine-jealousy view: spirit as object (creative spirit of Gen 2:7 or Holy Spirit), with “God” supplied as subject of both *epipothei* and *katōkisen*. Grammar favors divine jealousy; that forces *phthonos* = positive “jealousy.”  
- **Quote:** “On the whole, this issue is most naturally resolved in favor of the \"divine jealousy\" interpretation. It makes best grammatical sense to take \"God\" as the subject of both the main verb - epipothei, \"desire,\" \"yearn\" - and the subordinate verb - katgkisen, \"cause to dwell.\" But if God is the subject of \"desire,\" then this desire must obviously be a positive yearning; and this means, in turn, that phthonos must mean \"jealousy\" rather than \"envy.\""  
- **Locus:** Moo on Jas 4:5; cache ¶¶10–11  

### C-R5-008
- **Topic:** 4:5 ambiguity 2 — *phthonos* usually against divine reference  
- **Claim (Moo):** Lexical evidence for *phthonos* favors human envy: always negative in biblical Greek, never used of God; key term in the 3:13–4:3 tradition for sinful human attitude.  
- **Quote:** “And this issue undoubtedly favors the \"human envy\" interpretation. For phthonos always has a negative connotation in biblical Greek and is naturally never used with reference to God. Moreover, as we have seen, phthonos is a key word in the tradition that James has used in 3:13-4:3, and in this tradition the word always describes a sinful human attitude.”  
- **Locus:** Moo on Jas 4:5; cache ¶12  

### C-R5-009
- **Topic:** 4:5 ambiguity 3 — *epipotheō pros* indecisive  
- **Claim (Moo):** Human-envy needs “tend toward” (*pros* OK; “tend” unnatural for the verb). Divine-jealousy keeps normal “desire/yearn” but takes *pros* adverbially “in a jealous manner.” *Epipotheō* never of God in biblical Greek (favors human envy) but always positive in the NT (favors divine jealousy).  
- **Quote:** “The three key exegetical details therefore point in different directions. The grammar of the sentence (point one) favors the \"divine jealousy\" view; the meaning of phthonos (point two) the \"human envy\" interpretation; and favoring neither clearly is the third issue, the construction epipotheo pros.”  
- **Locus:** Moo on Jas 4:5; cache ¶¶13–14  

### C-R5-010
- **Topic:** 4:5 Moo’s verdict — divine jealousy via context  
- **Claim (Moo):** Exegetical data are not conclusive; *phthonos*/*zēlos* interchangeability and occasional Greek use of *phthonos* for Olympian gods make divine *phthonos* unusual but possible. Context decides: v. 5 substantiates v. 4’s spiritual adultery against the true “spouse,” so divine jealousy is “decisive.”  
- **Quote:** “Since, therefore, in our view the exegetical data of the verse are not conclusive, context becomes a key deciding factor. … But the immediate context provides strong, and, in our opinion, decisive, support for the \"divine jealousy\" interpretation. Verse 5 clearly substantiates a point made in v. 4. And v. 4 focuses on the spiritual adultery that James's readers are committing by following the world in distinction from their only true \"spouse,\" the Lord.”  
- **Locus:** Moo on Jas 4:5; cache ¶¶14–15  

### C-R5-011
- **Topic:** 4:5 “spirit” — creative spirit slightly preferred over Holy Spirit  
- **Claim (Moo):** Unclear whether “the spirit that he has made to dwell in us” is the Holy Spirit or God’s creative spirit (Gen 2:7); the latter slightly more likely because James never elsewhere mentions the Holy Spirit; either way God has a claim on us by his work in our lives.  
- **Quote:** “Perhaps the latter is slightly more likely, however, since James never elsewhere refers to the Holy Spirit. In either case, the phrase reminds us that God has a claim on us by virtue of his work in our lives.”  
- **Locus:** Moo on Jas 4:5; cache ¶16  

### C-R5-012
- **Topic:** 4:5 “Scripture” = theme of God’s jealousy, not a lost apocryphon  
- **Claim (Moo):** The “quotation” matches no OT or noncanonical Jewish text; many posit a lost apocryphon, but NT *graphē* is limited to canonical OT. On divine-jealousy reading, OT support is abundant (Exod 20:5; 34:14; Zech 8:2). Singular “scripture” need not force one verse (cf. John 7:37–39 theme); Moo identifies *graphē* here as the biblical theme of God’s jealousy for his people.  
- **Quote:** “Many scholars therefore suppose that James is citing a lost apocryphal text. But scripture (graphe) is limited to references to the canonical OT in the NT. … This being so, we can identify that which graphe speaks about as the biblical theme of God's jealousy for his people.”  
- **Locus:** Moo on Jas 4:5; cache ¶17  

### C-R5-013
- **Topic:** 4:6 “more grace” under divine-jealousy reading  
- **Claim (Moo):** If v. 5 is divine jealousy, “more/greater (*meizona*) grace” means God’s grace adequately meets the demands of that jealousy—“God gives what he demands” (Augustine). Human-envy reading would make grace the power to overcome sinfulness.  
- **Quote:** “If, however, as we have argued, v. 5 depicts God's jealousy for his people, then James here is reminding us that God's grace is completely adequate to meet the requirements imposed on us by that jealousy. … As Augustine has said, \"God gives what he demands.\""  
- **Locus:** Moo on Jas 4:6a; cache ¶18  

### C-R5-014
- **Topic:** 4:6 Prov 3:34 — grace to the humble; link to 1 Pet 5:5  
- **Claim (Moo):** Grace demands humility; James quotes Prov 3:34 (“God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble”), also in 1 Pet 5:5; humility dominates 4:7–10; sustaining grace only for those who admit need; pride often linked to jealousy/envy in Hellenistic writings, possibly condemning 3:13–4:3 attitudes.  
- **Quote:** “God's grace demands response: the response of humility. James introduces this note via his quotation from Prov. 3:34: \"God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.\" (This text is quoted also in 1 Pet. 5:5, another example of the close relationship between James and 1 Peter.) The humility introduced in this quotation becomes the dominant motif in the commands in vv. 7-10.”  
- **Locus:** Moo on Jas 4:6b; cache ¶19  

### C-R5-015
- **Topic:** 4:7–10 inclusio of submit / humble yourselves  
- **Claim (Moo):** Commands 7–10 flow from Prov 3:34; bookended by “submit yourselves to God” (7a) and “humble yourselves before the Lord” (10)—*tapeinoō* roots in *tapeinos* of the proverb—with structured commands between unpacking submission. Parallel structure to 1 Pet 5:5–9 may reflect a widespread early Christian repentance call.  
- **Quote:** “And, while not related verbally (the Greek verbs are different), submit yourselves to God and humble yourselves before the Lord are conceptually similar, forming an inclusio. … What James writes in vv. 6-10 is strikingly similar to 1 Pet. 5:5-9. … These parallels suggest that what James says here may reflect a widespread early Christian call to repentance.”  
- **Locus:** Moo on Jas 4:7–10; cache ¶¶20–21  

### C-R5-016
- **Topic:** Submit to God = place under lordship  
- **Claim (Moo):** *Hypotassō* = “put in order under”; to submit is glad recognition of God’s lordship and commitment to obey in all things.  
- **Quote:** “To submit to God means to place ourselves under his lordship, and therefore to commit ourselves to obey him in all things. The Greek verb (hypotasso) means to \"put in order under\" … Christians, James suggests, are even now to recognize God's lordship and to place ourselves in glad submission under his wise rule.”  
- **Locus:** Moo on Jas 4:7a; cache ¶22  

### C-R5-017
- **Topic:** Resist the devil — he will flee  
- **Claim (Moo):** First couplet unpacks submission: resist (*stand against*) the devil (*diabolos* = LXX for *sāṭān*, purpose “to separate God and man”); promise: he will flee; Christian has ability to overcome Satan’s power.  
- **Quote:** “Placing ourselves under God's authority means, negatively, that we firmly refuse to bow to the devil's authority. … When we resist the devil's purposes, he will, James promises, flee from you. … Whatever power Satan may have, the Christian can be absolutely certain that he has been given the ability to overcome that power.”  
- **Locus:** Moo on Jas 4:7b; cache ¶23  

### C-R5-018
- **Topic:** Draw near to God — restoration, not initial salvation  
- **Claim (Moo):** Positive parallel: “Come near to God and he will come near to you.” *Engizō* not primarily cultic worship here (Hos 12:6; T. Dan 6:2) but repentance/seeking God within submission; promise is restoration of Christian fellowship, not conversion of unbelievers (prodigal-father image).  
- **Quote:** “James is urging that we repent of our sins and seek God as an important aspect of his overall call to \"submit\" ourselves to God (v. 7). The promise that God will come near to those who come near to him does not, of course, apply to the salvation of unbelievers but to the restoration to fellowship of Christians.”  
- **Locus:** Moo on Jas 4:8a; cache ¶24  

### C-R5-019
- **Topic:** Wash hands / purify hearts — double-minded (*dipsychos*)  
- **Claim (Moo):** Parallel pejorative addresses (“sinners” / “double-minded”) echo “adulterous people”; *dipsychos* (possibly coined by James; cf. 1:8) marks trying to be friends with God and world at once—intolerable to jealous God (v. 5). Hands = external deeds; hearts = internal attitude; washing/purifying from cultic purity language applied ethically (cf. Ps 24:3–4).  
- **Quote:** "\"Double-souled,\" NIV double-minded (Gk. dipsychos), captures a key motif of the letter as a whole. … Its repetition here underscores especially James's accusation that his readers are attempting to be \"friends\" with both God and the world at the same time (v. 4): a conflict of basic allegiance that our jealous God will simply not tolerate (v. 5). … They must repent of both this external behavior - wash your hands - and the internal attitude that leads to such behavior - purify your hearts.”  
- **Locus:** Moo on Jas 4:8b; cache ¶26; links `double-mindedness`  

### C-R5-020
- **Topic:** 4:9 grieve/mourn/wail; laughter to mourning  
- **Claim (Moo):** Prophetic repentance language (Joel 2:12; imminent judgment 5:8); laughter as fool’s carefree hedonism of “friends with the world” (Prov; Luke 6:25b); counters casual attitude toward sin; “joy into gloom” is not opposed to Phil 4:4 joy of forgiveness but to superficial joy in sin.  
- **Quote:** “A carefree, \"devil-may-care\" attitude is typical of those who are \"friends with the world.\" … James's insistence that we turn our \"joy into gloom\" might sound strange in light of Paul's injunction to \"rejoice in the Lord always\" (Phil. 4:4). But the joy Paul speaks about is the joy that comes when we realize that our sins are forgiven in Christ; the joy James warns about is the fleeting and superficial joy that comes when we indulge in sin.”  
- **Locus:** Moo on Jas 4:9; cache ¶¶27–28  

### C-R5-021
- **Topic:** 4:10 humble yourselves — the Lord will lift up  
- **Claim (Moo):** Final command returns to Prov 3:34 springboard: recognize spiritual poverty, need of help, submit to God’s will; tax-collector parable / early-church motto (Luke 18:14); spiritual victory by giving self to the Lord, not self-exaltation (cf. 1:9–10).  
- **Quote:** “To \"humble ourselves before the Lord\" means to recognize our own spiritual poverty, to acknowledge consequently our desperate need of God's help, and to submit to his commanding will for our lives. … It reminds us that we gain spiritual vitality and victory not through our own strength or effort but through giving ourselves completely to the Lord.”  
- **Locus:** Moo on Jas 4:10; cache ¶29  

### C-R5-022
- **Topic:** 4:11–12 placement — speech inclusio closing 3:1–4:12  
- **Claim (Moo):** Against attaching 4:11–12 mainly to what follows (Cargal, Johnson, Martin), Moo takes them with the preceding community-conflict material: *katalalia* linked to pride God resists (4:6), jealousy, selfishness, quarrels, double-mindedness; possible Lev 19:16 near the love command; brief “reprise” of 3:1–12 so speech inclusio frames 3:1–4:12.  
- **Quote:** “Perhaps vv. 11-12 should be seen as a brief \"reprise\" of the larger discussion of sins of speech that opened the section (3:1-12). We would then have an inclusio on speech that frames the section 3:1-4:12.”  
- **Locus:** Moo on Jas 4:11–12 intro; cache ¶31  

### C-R5-023
- **Topic:** Do not slander — *katalaleō* / return to “brothers”  
- **Claim (Moo):** Harsh addresses of 4:4, 8 give way to “brothers”; *katalaleō* = “speak against” covers many harmful speech types; divisions of 3:13–4:3 likely explain the problem.  
- **Quote:** “The harsh, denunciatory address of 4:4 - adulterous people - and of 4:8 - sinners and double-minded - gives way here to James's more familiar brothers. … He begins with a prohibition of slander. This word translates a Greek word (katalaleo) that means, literally, \"speak against.\" … Quarrels over most issues usually end up including personal attacks and judgmental attitudes.”  
- **Locus:** Moo on Jas 4:11a; cache ¶32  

### C-R5-024
- **Topic:** Slander judges the law — royal/kingdom law (Lev 19)  
- **Claim (Moo):** Speaking against/judging a brother speaks against and judges the law—probably OT law taken into Jesus’ “law of the kingdom,” with Lev 19:16 (slander) near 19:18 love command (2:8). Criticism of a believer contradicts love of neighbor; failure to keep the law is “judging” it (denying its authority by not doing it).  
- **Quote:** “When James speaks of the law here, then, we are probably justified in thinking that he refers to the OT law insofar as it has been taken up into the \"law of the kingdom\" that Jesus laid upon his followers. … So James assumes that criticism of a fellow believer contradicts the demand that we love our neighbors. … Since James contrasts \"judging\" the law with \"keeping\" it, he apparently thinks that failure to do the law implies a denial of the law's authority.”  
- **Locus:** Moo on Jas 4:11b; cache ¶¶33–34  

### C-R5-025
- **Topic:** One Lawgiver and Judge — ultimate destiny only God’s  
- **Claim (Moo):** Slander also usurps God’s unique right as sole Lawgiver and Judge able to save and destroy (ultimate spiritual destiny; Matt 10:28); “who are you to judge your neighbor?” anchors love command. Not forbidding all discrimination or community discipline (1 Cor 5–6), but jealous censorious speech that condemns others as wrong before God (cf. Rom 14).  
- **Quote:** “James therefore is thinking of \"judging\" in terms of determining the ultimate spiritual destiny of individuals. And the believer has no right to make any such determination: But you - who are you to judge your neighbor? … James is not prohibiting the proper, and necessary, discrimination that every Christian should exercise. Nor is he forbidding the right of the community to exclude from its fellowship those it deems to be in flagrant disobedience … James rebukes jealous, censorious speech by which we condemn others as being wrong in the sight of God.”  
- **Locus:** Moo on Jas 4:12; cache ¶¶35–36  

### C-R5-026
- **Topic:** Transition at 4:13 — unit 4:13–5:11 as clash of worldviews  
- **Claim (Moo):** Transition at 4:13 (not 4:6/4:11): 4:11–12 inclusio with 3:1–12; 4:13 // 5:1 address formulas; both rebuke well-to-do arrogance without God/eternity. Loose unity of 4:13–5:11: godless worldview (boastful self-reliance 4:13–17; selfish indulgence 5:1–6) vs biblical worldview (providence 4:15; coming judgment/reward 5:1, 3, 5, 7). 5:7–11 is the faithful response to that arrogance.  
- **Quote:** “The underlying issue that brings loose unity to 4:13-5:11 is a clash of worldviews. We find, on the one hand, a worldview that largely leaves God out of account, marked by boastful self-reliance (4:13-17) and selfish indulgence (5:1-6). … Faithful Christians, James urges, must respond with a resolute reaffirmation of the biblical worldview, marked by God's constant providential ordering of events (4:15) and the reality of a coming day on which God will reward the faithful and punish the sinful (5:1, 3, 5, 7).”  
- **Locus:** Moo on Jas 4:13–5:11 structure; cache ¶¶37–39  

### C-R5-027
- **Topic:** 4:13–17 merchants = relatively well-to-do Christian merchants  
- **Claim (Moo):** Never called “rich,” but travel and “make money” mark merchant class. Unlike 5:1–6’s non-Christian rich under unrelieved condemnation, 4:13–17 chastises failure of Christian perspective (vv. 14–15, 17)—James returns to 1:10–11: rich believers must not boast in worldly accomplishments.  
- **Quote:** “James would hardly address non-Christians in this way. It is just at this point that 5:1-6 differs from 4:13-17: James pronounces a verdict of condemnation on the \"rich\" of 5:1 with no hint that their fate might be avoided. In 4:13-17, then, James returns to the theme of 1:10-11, encouraging rich believers to avoid boasting in their own worldly accomplishments and to put their trust in the Lord.”  
- **Locus:** Moo on Jas 4:13 intro; cache ¶41  

### C-R5-028
- **Topic:** Not anti-capitalism or anti-planning — anti-arrogant self-confidence  
- **Claim (Moo):** Fictional speech of self-confident planners sure they will make money; not a rebuke of profit as such or of all future planning (life insurance/retirement can be stewardship); rebuke is this-worldly self-confidence that we can determine the future (v. 16).  
- **Quote:** “James is not rebuking these merchants for their plans or even for their desire to make a profit. He rebukes them rather for the this-worldly self-confidence that they exhibit in pursuing these goals … What James rebukes here, as v. 16 will make clear, is any kind of planning for the future that stems from human arrogance in our ability to determine the course of future events.”  
- **Locus:** Moo on Jas 4:13; cache ¶¶43–44  

### C-R5-029
- **Topic:** Life as mist/vapor — transitory  
- **Claim (Moo):** *Hoitines* qualitative: “people such as you” cannot dictate the future. Prefers NIV-style punctuation (assertion + “What is your life?”). Life = *atmis* mist/smoke/vapor—insubstantial; illness, accident, or Christ’s return can end it like morning sun on mist.  
- **Quote:** “You are a mist that appears for a little while and then vanishes. \"Mist\" translates a relatively rare word within biblical Greek (atmis), which can also be rendered \"smoke\" … or even \"vapor\" … human life is insubstantial and transitory, here one minute and gone the next.”  
- **Locus:** Moo on Jas 4:14; cache ¶¶45–46  

### C-R5-030
- **Topic:** “If the Lord wills” — *conditio Jacobaea*; attitude not magic formula  
- **Claim (Moo):** “Instead” links to v. 13; add “If it is the Lord’s will” (*conditio Jacobaea*). “Lord” likely God the Father (usual for James), baptizing a common religious proverb into biblical providence. Better mss: “live” in apodosis—continuance of life itself contingent on the Lord. Not verbal formula magic (Calvin: principle fixed in mind); evaluate plans by contingency and biblical ethics.  
- **Quote:** “James urges these confident and presumptuous merchants to add a key qualifier to their planning: \"If it is the Lord's will.\" This explicit expression of dependence on the Lord has come to be known as the \"Jacobean condition\" (conditio Jacobaea) … \"If the Lord wills\" can become nothing more than a glib formula without any real meaning. James, rather, wants us to adopt the attitude expressed by the words as a fixed perspective from which to view all of life.”  
- **Locus:** Moo on Jas 4:15; cache ¶¶48–50  

### C-R5-031
- **Topic:** 4:16 boasting in arrogances — worldly self-sufficiency  
- **Claim (Moo):** Root problem is arrogance: Greek “you boast in your arrogances”; *kauchaomai* is not always negative—problem is misplaced pride in charting the future / “pride of life” (cf. 1 John). All such boasting is evil; Christians warned against world’s mold of autonomy (Greek *hybris*).  
- **Quote:** “And the root problem is arrogance: you boast and brag. … It is this \"pride of life,\" this arrogant sense of self-sufficiency so characteristic of the world, that James condemns in this passage. All such boasting is evil, James concludes. … Such an attitude is simply inconsistent with a Christian worldview in which there is a God who sovereignly directs the course of human affairs.”  
- **Locus:** Moo on Jas 4:16; cache ¶¶51–52  

### C-R5-032
- **Topic:** 4:17 sin of omission  
- **Claim (Moo):** Traditional-sounding saying linked by *oun*: having been told to reckon with the Lord in planning (v. 15), failure to do so is sin—sins of omission as serious as commission (Luke 12:47; 19:11–27; Matt 25:31–46). Not primarily about failure to use money for good (not yet wealth per se).  
- **Quote:** “So probably we are to posit a more general connection between v. 17 and what James has commanded us to do in v. 15. He has urged us to take the Lord into consideration in all our planning. We therefore have no excuse in this matter: we know what we are to do. To fail now to do it, James wants to make clear, is sin. … As Scripture makes abundantly clear, sins of omission are as real and serious as sins of commission.”  
- **Locus:** Moo on Jas 4:17; cache ¶¶53–54  

### C-R5-033
- **Topic:** 5:1–6 non-Christian rich landowners; prophetic doom style  
- **Claim (Moo):** Closely related to 4:13–17 (same *age nyn*; wealth without God) but differences greater: no diatribe/exhortation—unrelieved prophetic doom on pagan-style targets. Wealthy landowners (v. 4); condemned for sinful use of wealth, not wealth alone; addressed to church so faithful won’t envy and will trust God as avenger (Calvin).  
- **Quote:** “James 5:1-6, however, has none of that. James's style is that of the prophets pronouncing doom on pagan nations. He unrelievedly attacks these people, with no hint of exhortation. … You rich people, as we have argued in the introduction to this section, are not among the (Christian) readers of the letter. They are, rather, wealthy non-Christians who are oppressing the Christian community.”  
- **Locus:** Moo on Jas 5:1–6 intro; cache ¶¶57–60  

### C-R5-034
- **Topic:** Structure of 5:1–6 — four grounds of condemnation  
- **Claim (Moo):** Governing announcement of condemnation (v. 1); reasons: (1) selfish hoarding (2–3); (2) defrauding workers (4); (3) self-indulgent lifestyle (5); (4) oppressing “the righteous” (6). “Misery” = eschatological judgment (plural), not mere temporal hardship; *klaiō* + *ololyzo* prophetic day-of-the-Lord language.  
- **Quote:** “Governing the passage is James's announcement of condemnation on the \"rich\" (v. 1). He then explains why these rich people are destined for condemnation: (1) they have selfishly hoarded wealth (vv. 2-3); (2) they have defrauded their workers (v. 4); (3) they follow a self-indulgent lifestyle (v. 5); and (4) they oppress \"the righteous\" (v. 6). … This background makes clear that the misery that is coming upon the rich refers not to earthly, temporal suffering, but to the condemnation and punishment that God will mete out to them on the day of judgment.”  
- **Locus:** Moo on Jas 5:1–6 structure / 5:1; cache ¶¶59, 61  

### C-R5-035
- **Topic:** “Rich” as theological–economic; caution for Western readers  
- **Claim (Moo):** Biblical “rich” often merges economic and theological (“unrighteous”); NT almost always condemns misuse; 1:10 implies some rich Christians exist—so not all rich people judged. Still, wealth easily associates with unrighteousness (Matt 19:23); Western Christians must ask “When do we have too much?”  
- **Quote:** “The designation you rich in verse 1, therefore, essentially means, as so often in Scripture, the unrighteous rich. But, having said this, we must caution against a tendency for Western Christians (most of whom are \"wealthy\" in comparative terms) to dismiss as entirely irrelevant the teaching of a paragraph like this. … Scripture warns that wealth can be a particularly strong obstacle to Christian discipleship.”  
- **Locus:** Moo on Jas 5:1; cache ¶¶58, 62  

### C-R5-036
- **Topic:** Hoarded wealth as witness; treasure in the last days  
- **Claim (Moo):** Rotted wealth / moth-eaten clothes / corroded gold-silver will testify against and “eat your flesh like fire” (judgment). Hoarding shows false priorities and deprives others of life (Sir 29; Luke 12:33; Calvin). “You have hoarded wealth in the last days”: *en* = “in” present era of fulfillment, not merely “for” future judgment—piling wealth “in an age that is near its close” (REB), ignoring grace already shown and judgment near (like rich fool).  
- **Quote:** “What James is saying, then, is that those who are avidly accumulating wealth in his day are particularly sinful because they utterly disregard the demands made upon people by the display of God's grace in Christ, and especially foolish because they ignore the many signs of the rapidly approaching judgment. The REB captures the idea very well: \"You have piled up wealth in an age that is near its close.\""  
- **Locus:** Moo on Jas 5:2–3; cache ¶¶63, 65–66  

### C-R5-037
- **Topic:** Unpaid wages cry out to the Lord of hosts  
- **Claim (Moo):** Second accusation: cheating hired workers of pay (*apostereō* preferred; Mal 3:5; Lev 19:13; Deut 24:14–15). First-century land concentration forced day laborers; withholding pay could jeopardize life. Wages “cry out” (Deut 24:15; Gen 4:10 blood imagery); known to “Lord Almighty” (*sabaoth*, Lord of hosts)—holy, powerful, determined to judge oppression.  
- **Quote:** “Not so the second: they have cheated their workers of their pay. … In a society where credit was not readily available, the failure to pay workers promptly could jeopardize life itself. … In an echo of Deut. 24:15 … James claims that the wages themselves are crying out against you. … What the rich think they do in secret, and without danger of prosecution, is not hidden from the Lord Almighty.”  
- **Locus:** Moo on Jas 5:4; cache ¶¶67–68  

### C-R5-038
- **Topic:** Luxury and self-indulgence; “day of slaughter” = day of judgment  
- **Claim (Moo):** Third reason: lived in luxury and self-indulgence (*tryphaō* + *spatalaō*; “on earth” contrasts this-life ease with coming torment; Luke 16:25). “Fattened yourselves in the day of slaughter” = eschatological judgment (not only any time of reverse fortune; not primarily A.D. 70)—like cattle fattened for the kill while judgment impends; parallel to hoarding “in the last days.”  
- **Quote:** “It is, therefore, far more likely that the day of slaughter is a vivid description of the day of judgment. … James's point then, as in v. 3, is that the rich are selfishly and ignorantly going about accumulating wealth for themselves and wastefully spending it on their own pleasures in the very day when God's judgment is imminently threatened. … They are like cattle being fattened for the kill.”  
- **Locus:** Moo on Jas 5:5; cache ¶¶69–70  

### C-R5-039
- **Topic:** Condemned/murdered “the righteous one” — general poor victim  
- **Claim (Moo):** Climax: condemned and murdered “the righteous one” (*ton dikaion*)—not Jesus or (pseudonymous) James the Just, but the typical righteous sufferer; *katadikazō* suggests judicial misuse of wealth/influence (Wis 2; Amos; Micah; Jas 2:5–7). “Murder” = practical outcome of cheating land and livelihood (Sir 34:22). Final clause best as statement of nonresistance of the helpless poor (not “Does God not resist you?”).  
- **Quote:** “\"The righteous one\" is the typical follower of God, experiencing persecution at the hands of the wicked rich. … But how can James claim that the rich have murdered innocent men? He probably has in mind the practical outcome of the actions that the rich take against the poor to cheat them of their land and take away their gainful employment: the poor starve to death. … On the whole, then, the usual view is best: James, \"on a note of majestic pathos,\" concludes the paragraph by reminding us that the righteous are helpless victims of the stratagems of the rich and powerful.”  
- **Locus:** Moo on Jas 5:6; cache ¶¶71–72  

### C-R5-040
- **Topic:** 5:7–11 patience theme as flip side of 5:1–6  
- **Claim (Moo):** Return of “brothers” (vv. 7, 9, 10); dominant vocabulary: *makrothymeō/makrothymia* and *hypomenō/hypomonē*. Therefore (*oun*) after denunciation of rich: be patient until the Lord’s *parousia* (Jesus’ return as judge and savior, technical early-Christian sense). Pattern like Psalm 37: do not envy wicked prosperity; wait for God’s vindication.  
- **Quote:** “The then (Gk. oun, \"therefore\") shows that James views his admonition to believers … as a logical consequence of his denunciation of the wicked rich in 5:1-6. … James certainly intends, and his readers would certainly have understood, the Lord's coming to refer to Jesus' return as judge and savior. … James's advice is the same as the psalmist's: \"be patient,\" for the \"coming of the Lord,\" when the wicked will be judged (5:1-6) and the righteous delivered, \"is near.\""  
- **Locus:** Moo on Jas 5:7 intro; cache ¶¶74–76  

### C-R5-041
- **Topic:** Patience until the Lord — farmer illustration  
- **Claim (Moo):** *Makrothymia* here overlaps *hypomonē* (not a neat people-vs-circumstances split). “Until” is pregnant: wait for and look for the coming; implicit ban on private vengeance (Rom 12:19). Farmer waits for valuable crop dependent on early and later rains (Deut 11:14 etc.); OT “early and later rains” contexts affirm the Lord’s faithfulness—echo reinforcing confidence in the Lord’s coming.  
- **Quote:** “Until (hens) has a \"pregnant\" sense, suggesting the idea of a goal as well as a time period: \"exercise patience as you wait for, and look for, the coming of the Lord.\" … Every reference to \"early and later rains\" in the OT occurs in a context affirming the faithfulness of the Lord … James's readers, being biblically literate, would have detected in the language of this verse an \"echo\" of this broader biblical theme and been thereby given a further reinforcement of the confidence they could place in the coming of the Lord to judge their enemies and deliver them.”  
- **Locus:** Moo on Jas 5:7; cache ¶¶77–78  

### C-R5-042
- **Topic:** Stand firm; nearness of the parousia (imminent, not dating error)  
- **Claim (Moo):** “Stand firm” = “strengthen your hearts”—firm adherence in trials. Nearness (*engizō*) of the Lord’s coming: Moo rejects “delay of the parousia made them wrong” for those affirming NT truthfulness; within salvation history, last days inaugurated at death/resurrection/Spirit; length unknown (Mark 13:32); return is always “next event,” hence “near”/imminent for every generation.  
- **Quote:** “With the death and resurrection of Jesus and pouring out of the Spirit, the \"last days\" have been inaugurated. … the length of this age is unknown. Not even Jesus knew how long the \"last days\" would last (cf. Mark 13:32). What this means is that the return of Christ, as the next event in the salvation-historical timetable, is, from the time of the early church to our own day, \"near,\" or \"imminent.\" … we need to be patient and stand firm, because the Lord's coming is near.”  
- **Locus:** Moo on Jas 5:8; cache ¶¶79–81  

### C-R5-043
- **Topic:** 5:9 do not grumble — Judge at the door  
- **Claim (Moo):** Fits context via imminence + community patience: *stenazō* “grumble/groan” against one another under oppression; unlike 4:11–12 (critical speech = judging), here criticism places one in danger of judgment (Matt 7:1). Parousia comfort against wicked becomes also assessment of believers—“The coming Lord is also the judge of the Christian” (Davids, cited approvingly).  
- **Quote:** “As he did in 4:11-12, James connects the need to refrain from critical speech with judgment. In the former passage, however, he likened critical speech to judgment; here he warns that criticism of one another places a person in danger of judgment. … We should note the striking shift in application of parousia language in these verses. … \"The coming Lord is also the judge of the Christian.\""  
- **Locus:** Moo on Jas 5:9; cache ¶¶82–84  

### C-R5-044
- **Topic:** Prophets as example of suffering and patience  
- **Claim (Moo):** Martyrological tradition after Maccabees (*hypodeigma* in 2/4 Macc); tentatively render “example of suffering and patience” (not only hendiadys). Unspecified prophets (Jeremiah; Isaiah sawn, Heb 11:37 tradition); they spoke “in the name of the Lord”—doing God’s will often brings suffering; may also model speaking against injustice while waiting for vindication.  
- **Quote:** “James urges his readers to take the prophets who spoke in the name of the Lord as an example of patience in the face of suffering. … We tentatively opt, then, for the rendering \"example of suffering and patience.\" … Doing God's will, James is suggesting, will often lead to suffering. … Christians need to learn to suffer patiently as they await the Lord's vindication. But this is not to say that they cannot speak out against evil.”  
- **Locus:** Moo on Jas 5:10; cache ¶¶85–87  

### C-R5-045
- **Topic:** Blessed who have persevered; Job; *telos* of the Lord  
- **Claim (Moo):** Blessing those who persevered echoes Maccabean and Jesus (Matt 5:11–12) and 1:12 (*makarizo* rare). Job is a curious model (canonical Job complains), but *Testament of Job* and Job’s unbroken faith (1:21; 2:10; 19:25–27) support perseverance. *Telos kyriou*: reject Christ’s death or parousia as “end”; between restorative “end” God brought about for Job (NIV-style) and “purpose” of refining (NJB/NASB/NRSV), Moo prefers restorative end—leads into “The Lord is full of compassion and mercy”; not a promise of material prosperity always, but blessing from merciful God for patient endurance.  
- **Quote:** “A literal rendering of these words would be \"you have seen the telos of the Lord.\" … This latter interpretation [restorative end in Job’s situation] should probably be adopted. … Your present suffering, James would be saying, is not the \"end\" of the story; God will transform your situation for good when Christ is revealed in glory. … Of course, James does not mean that patience in suffering will always be rewarded by material prosperity … But James does seek to encourage our faithful, patient endurance of affliction by reminding us of the blessing that we receive for such faithfulness from our merciful and compassionate God.”  
- **Locus:** Moo on Jas 5:11; cache ¶¶88–91, 97  

### C-R5-046
- **Topic:** Summary synthesis of 4:4–10 (Moo’s own wrap in 4:11–12 discussion)  
- **Claim (Moo):** Community disputes fueled by bitter selfish spirit and unrestrained tongue manifest worldly spirit (3:15; 4:1, 4), incompatible with God’s jealous desire for wholehearted allegiance (4:4–5); yet God bestows favor if pride yields to deep repentance and abasement (4:6–10).  
- **Quote:** “This flirtation with the world must be seen to be incompatible with God's jealous desire to have his people's wholehearted allegiance (4:4-5). Yet God is willing to turn and bestow his favor if sinful pride can give way to deep-felt repentance and sincere abasement before him (4:6-10).”  
- **Locus:** Moo concluding 3:13–4:12 thread at 4:12; cache ¶36  

### C-R5-047
- **Topic:** Liberation-theology reception of 5:1–6 (Moo’s caution)  
- **Claim (Moo):** James’s forthright denunciation of the rich has made him a key biblical spokesperson for liberation theology; Moo accepts social critique of greedy landowners but insists “rich” needs careful economic–theological definition and that condemnation targets sinful use, not wealth as such—while still pressing the selfish-accumulation question on Western Christians.  
- **Quote:** “And, in so forthrightly denouncing the \"rich,\" James has become a key biblical spokesperson for the liberation theology movement. However, as we pointed out in the exposition of 1:10-11, the term \"rich\" must be carefully defined in the biblical context. … What can be said about the \"rich\" in this passage, however, is that they are condemned not simply for their wealth; they are condemned for their sinful use of wealth. … One of the sins for which God condemns these people is their selfish accumulation of money and things (vv. 2-3). … When do we have too much?”  
- **Locus:** Moo on Jas 5:1–6 intro; cache ¶58  

### C-R5-048
- **Topic:** *Dipsychos* and overlap of ages  
- **Claim (Moo):** Double-mindedness is the Christian problem of living in the “overlap” of the ages—pulled between Christ’s kingdom and Satan’s, Spirit and flesh—when the world entices away from single-minded allegiance.  
- **Quote:** “The Christian, living in the \"overlap\" of the ages, is pulled between the kingdom of Christ and the kingdom of Satan, the realm of Spirit and the realm of \"flesh.\" To allow \"the world\" to entice us away from total, single-minded allegiance to God is to become people who are divided in loyalties, \"double-minded\" and spiritually unstable.”  
- **Locus:** Moo on Jas 4:8; cache ¶26; links `double-mindedness`  

### C-R5-049
- **Topic:** 4:13–17 // 5:1–6 addressees distinguished again in 5:7 intro  
- **Claim (Moo):** Explicit reiteration: 4:13–17 = overly self-confident Christian businesspeople; 5:1–6 = non-Christian rich; both lack “brothers”; 5:7–11 focuses attitudes of God’s people under biblical worldview and coming judgment.  
- **Quote:** “Overly self-confident Christian businesspeople are probably in view in 4:13-17, whereas the non-Christian rich are James's target in 5:1-6. But both paragraphs lack James's customary address to his readers, \"brothers.\" This changes in 5:7-11 (vv. 7, 9, 10).”  
- **Locus:** Moo on Jas 5:7–11 intro; cache ¶74  

### C-R5-050
- **Topic:** Job’s perseverance not passive resignation (Barclay via Moo)  
- **Claim (Moo):** Job’s model is not “groveling, passive, unquestioning submission”; he struggled and questioned yet never extinguished faith—relevant for readers under trial.  
- **Quote:** “For although Job did complain bitterly about God's treatment of him, he never abandoned his faith. In the midst of his incomprehension, he clung to God and continued to hope in him (see 1:21; 2:10; 16:19-21; 19:25-27). As Barclay says, \"Job's is no groveling, passive, unquestioning submission; Job struggled and questioned, and sometimes even defied, but the flame of faith was never extinguished in his heart.\""  
- **Locus:** Moo on Jas 5:11 (Job); cache ¶90
